_note: 2.2.0 (over 2.1.0, which stays as it is): the slide titles and the speaker notes of the deck 5.2.0 (teach slides included), each slide tied to a concept by its example or its title; 47 slides tied.

slides.title: Loops
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter teaches repetition: while and for loops, range, the containers a loop visits, modules, and leaving a program early. Every concept has an idea, an everyday picture, the code and what the run printed. The same examples run on the chapter page.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts, each a run of slides you can jump to. Every code example sits in the chapter-code tab of the page in this same order. Example: part three has six examples about what a for loop visits. Ask the class: which part do you expect to be hardest, and why?

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions guide the chapter. What decides when a loop repeats and when it stops, and which statements leave or skip a pass? Which parts of the book differ in current Python? Example: break leaves, continue skips. Ask the class to guess the first answer now.

slides.title: Part 1: Repeating with while
slides.say: Part one. A while loop tests first, then runs its block. Watch the test turn False. Break and continue change the flow, and the walrus names a value inside the test. Predict the number of passes before each run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: repeating
slides.say: A washing machine repeats a cycle until the programme ends, and a guard decides at every round whether to walk another one. Example: the piggy bank is an accumulator. Ask the class to add one more everyday loop of their own, and name its stop condition.

slides.title: while: a test before every pass
slides.say: A while loop tests first, then runs its block, then tests again. Example: a guard who asks at every round whether the door is still open. Ask the class: what has to change inside the block so that the test one day turns False?

slides.title: while: repeat as long as the test is true
slides.say: Run the code and read the table pass by pass. Spam goes from zero to five, and the last test is False. Ask the class to predict the number of printed passes before the run, then check the table. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Accumulator: a total that grows
slides.say: An accumulator is a variable that remembers the result so far. Example: a piggy bank that gets one more coin at every pass. Ask the class: which value must the accumulator start with if you want a sum, and which if you want a product?

slides.title: An accumulator adds up 1 to 100
slides.say: The chart plots the running total at every twentieth number. The last value is 5050, the same as the formula gives. Ask the class to change the stop to 10 and predict the total before the run. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Story: Gauss added 1 to 100 without a loop
slides.say: The Gauss tale has a paper trail back to a memorial of 1856, and Brian Hayes collected the printed versions in American Scientist in 2006, so call it a legend. Both the loop and the formula give 5050. Ask the class: which would you trust for a million numbers?

slides.title: break: leave a loop at once
slides.say: While True is a loop with no test that ever fails, so a break must end it. Example: asking for a name until the right one is typed. Ask the class: what would happen if the program never reached the break line?

slides.title: while True runs until break leaves it
slides.say: Follow the three passes in the picture: two wrong answers, then Alice. The iterator stands in for the keyboard, so the page can run it. Ask the class to add a fourth answer after Alice and predict whether it is read.

slides.title: continue: skip the rest of one pass
slides.say: Continue ends one pass and goes back to the test. Example: skipping a song on a playlist. Ask the class: how is that different from break, and what would a break do to the list of shown numbers? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: continue skips the rest of one pass
slides.say: The picture colours the eight numbers: odd ones are shown, even ones are skipped. Ask the class to predict the two lists before the run, then to change the test so that multiples of three are skipped. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: The walrus: name a value in the test
slides.say: The walrus names a value inside an expression, so the read and the test are one step. Example: a cashier who says the total aloud and writes it down. Ask the class: why does the loop end when read gives an empty string?

slides.title: The assignment expression in a loop test
slides.say: The picture lists the four pieces that were read, and the empty string that ended the loop. The last piece is shorter because the text ran out. Ask the class to change five to three and predict the pieces. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Story: the walrus operator and PEP 572
slides.say: PEP 572 was created on 28 February 2018 and shipped in Python 3.8. Guido stepped down as benevolent dictator for life on 12 July 2018. Show the page of the proposal. Ask the class: when does naming a value inside a test help readability, and when does it hurt?

slides.title: Part 2: Counting with for and range
slides.say: Part two. For takes the items of a sequence one by one. Range describes numbers without storing them, and it stops before the stop value. Keep the school-year picture in mind.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: for and range
slides.say: The postman has a list and visits each house. Range is the list of house numbers, printed only on demand. A school year shows why a half-open interval has no overlaps. Example: the dealer's hand is an iterator. Question: what does the dealer do when the cards run out?

slides.title: for and range: one value per pass
slides.say: A for loop needs no counter: it takes the next value of range each time. Example: a postman who needs no counter, only his list. Ask the class: what are the values of i if you write range of five?

slides.title: for: one value of range(5) per pass
slides.say: The chart shows the total growing after each pass: zero, one, three, six, ten. The loop variable keeps its last value, four. Ask the class to change range of five to range of one, six and predict the final total.

slides.title: range: start, stop and step
slides.say: Range takes a stop, a start and a stop, or a start, a stop and a step. The stop is never included. Example: a school year that ends the day before the next one. Ask the class: how many items has range of ten, twenty?

slides.title: range(start, stop, step)
slides.say: The picture draws the four ranges as rows of numbers. Zero to three plus three to seven make zero to seven, so neighbours meet. Ask the class to write a range that gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 and check it.

slides.title: Story: why range stops before the end
slides.say: Dijkstra's memo EWD831 is dated 11 August 1982. Half-open ranges give the length as stop minus start and let neighbours meet without a gap. Show the memo on the archive page. Ask the class: how many items has range(10, 25)?

slides.title: range is lazy: a recipe, not a list
slides.say: A range keeps only a recipe and computes values on demand. Example: a ticket machine that prints a ticket when it is asked. Ask the class: why can len of a range of a billion be answered at once, while a list of a billion cannot even be built?

slides.title: range describes numbers; it does not store them
slides.say: The table shows five questions about a range of a billion, all answered at once. The slice is another range, not a list. Ask the class to explain in one sentence why the in test is arithmetic and not a search.

slides.title: Part 3: What a for loop visits
slides.say: Part three. A loop can visit lists, tuples and dictionaries. Enumerate and zip remove index arithmetic. Under every for sit iter and next, and an else clause can tell you that no break happened.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: what a loop visits
slides.say: A list changes like a shopping list, a tuple is fixed like a printed ticket, and a dictionary looks up by key like a phone book. Unpacking puts each part of a pair into its own name. Question: which container would you choose for the days of the week, and why?

slides.title: for visits a list and a tuple
slides.say: A for loop visits any ordered container the same way. Example: a shopping list and a printed ticket. Ask the class: what would Python do if the loop body tried to change a tuple item, and why? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: for visits a list and a tuple
slides.say: The chart shows the length of each pet name, and the tuple doubled. The loop code is the same for both. Ask the class to add a fourth pet to the list and predict the new chart. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: for visits the pairs of a dictionary
slides.say: Items gives key and value pairs, and the loop unpacks each pair into two names. Example: a phone book read as name and number together. Ask the class: what does a loop over the dictionary alone give you? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: for visits the pairs of a dictionary
slides.say: The chart shows the three ages. The second line prints the sum of the values and the list of keys. Ask the class to change the code so that it prints only the names with an age above three. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: enumerate and zip
slides.say: Enumerate adds a counter; zip walks two sequences side by side. Example: a roll call with numbers beside the names. Ask the class: why is that clearer than looping over range of len of the names? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: enumerate and zip replace index arithmetic
slides.say: The two tables show the numbered names and the name and score pairs. Notice that no index is written by hand. Ask the class to add a third list of grades and predict what zip of three lists gives. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: zip: silent stop or strict check
slides.say: Zip stops at the shorter list unless you ask for strict. Example: two lines of dancers of different length. Ask the class: which is worse in a real program, a silent drop or a loud error, and why? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: zip: stop silently, or insist on equal lengths
slides.say: The picture shows the pairs that were made, the error that strict raised, and the pairs that plain zip made. The three is dropped without a word. Ask the class to make the lists equal so that strict passes. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Under every for: iter and next
slides.say: An iterator remembers its place and gives the next item when next asks. Example: a dealer's hand of cards. Ask the class: what do you think a for loop does when next raises StopIteration? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: Under every for: iter and next
slides.say: The diagram shows iter, then next twice, then StopIteration. The last line shows that an iterator returns itself, but a list does not. Ask the class to predict what next gives a third time. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: else on a loop: no break happened
slides.say: The else of a loop runs only when the loop was not left by break. Example: a searcher who says the key is not in the house after checking every room. Ask the class: which of the two lists will reach the else, and why?

slides.title: break, and the else clause of a loop
slides.say: The picture follows both lists: the first breaks at eight, the second runs out. Only the second reaches the else. Ask the class to change the second list so that it contains an even number and predict the output. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Part 4: Modules and leaving early
slides.say: Part four. Import opens a module and keeps its names in a namespace. Sys.exit ends a program by raising an exception that carries the exit status. Think of the toolbox and the lift button.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: modules
slides.say: A module is a toolbox with a label, and a namespace keeps its names apart from yours like a street address. If no shop on the search path has the toolbox, Python says so. Example: math.sqrt. Question: what would a clash of two sqrt names look like?

slides.title: import: borrow a module, seed the dice
slides.say: Import opens a module, and a seed fixes the sequence of a random generator. Example: a bookmark in a book of random numbers. Ask the class: why would a teacher want a seeded program when grading homework? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: import random: a seeded dice roll
slides.say: The chart counts how often each die face came up in the six rolls. The last line shows that a module has a name and a type. Ask the class to change the seed and say what stays the same.

slides.title: Two import forms, two namespaces
slides.say: Import math keeps the module name in front; from-import copies one name, which may be renamed with as. Example: two houses on different streets, each with a kitchen. Ask the class: when is the first form safer? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: Two import forms, two namespaces
slides.say: The diagram shows two namespaces, one named math and one that is ours. Root is our name for the same function. Sqrt is missing from ours, hence the NameError. Ask the class to fix the error with one more import line.

slides.title: When import fails: the search path
slides.say: Python looks for a module in the folders of sys.path, one after the other. Example: visiting the shops on a list until one has the toolbox. Ask the class: what would you check first if an import of your own file fails?

slides.title: When import fails: the module search path
slides.say: The first printed line says that sys.path is a list and not empty. The second says which module is missing. Ask the class to import a real module such as math inside the try block and predict the output. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: leaving early
slides.say: Sys.exit is the stop button of a lift, and the exit status is the light that tells why it stopped. An exception interrupts normal flow like a fire alarm. The yellow road sign is the new Python 3.14 warning about finally. Question: when is status 0 right?

slides.title: sys.exit(): end a program with a status
slides.say: Sys.exit raises the exception SystemExit. Its argument is the exit status. Example: zero is the green light at the garage exit, any other number is red. Ask the class: why does the finally clause still run after sys.exit? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: sys.exit() ends a program with an exit status
slides.say: The picture follows the program: working, then the exit with status three, then the except clause, then finally. The line after sys.exit never ran. Ask the class to change the status to zero and predict what changes. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Part 5: Two short programs
slides.say: Part five. Two short programs from the book, with scripted input so that they run on the page. Predict the output first, then check it against the run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: short programs
slides.say: Both programs are small board games: a few rules, a loop of turns and a winner at the end. The summary and the practice questions close the chapter. Example: twenty questions is Guess the Number. Ask the class which game they would extend first, and how.

slides.title: Program: Guess the Number
slides.say: The program draws a secret and gives the player six guesses. Example: twenty questions about one number. Ask the class: which statement leaves the loop when the guess is right, and what does the variable taken hold afterwards? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: Guess the Number: at most six guesses
slides.say: The picture marks each guess on a line from low to high and shows where the secret is. The scripted guesses replace a typing player. Ask the class to change the guesses so that the player needs five passes. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Program: win or lose with for and else
slides.say: The else of the inner loop is the lose branch, so no flag variable is needed. Example: a treasure hunt that ends with a whistle. Ask the class: what has to happen so that the else line is printed? Draw the four steps on the board, then let one student retell them in their own words.

slides.title: Guess the Number: the ending, with for and else
slides.say: The chart shows how many guesses each of the two games used. The first game breaks after four guesses. The second runs through all six and reaches the else. Ask the class to make the first player win on guess two.

slides.title: Program: Rock, Paper, Scissors
slides.say: A dictionary holds the rule of the game, and one chain of tests turns two moves into three outcomes. Example: paper covers rock, so paper wins. Ask the class: which test comes first, and why must the tie come before the beats test?

slides.title: Rock, Paper, Scissors: one round
slides.say: The diagram shows the two moves, the rule and the result. Change the two moves in the code and the result changes with them. Ask the class to predict the result for scissors against paper and then run it. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Program: six rounds and a score
slides.say: The score is a dictionary with three accumulators, and the loop adds 1 to the one that matches. Example: a tally sheet with one stroke for every point. Ask the class: why is plus equals on a dictionary value a good fit here?

slides.title: Rock, Paper, Scissors: six rounds and a score
slides.say: The table lists the six rounds and the chart shows the final score. Two wins, two losses and two ties make six rounds. Ask the class to change one move and predict the new score before running it. Run the example on the chapter page and compare the run with the picture.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. The walrus came in 3.8 and strict zip in 3.10. Python 3.14 warns when return, break or continue leaves a finally block. Control-C stops an endless loop. Ask the class: which of these would you use first, and which Python do you run?

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples in each part of this chapter. Example: a for loop takes any iterable, and range stops before its stop value. Ask the class: which sentence would you teach to a friend first, and what example would you show?

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run them on the chapter page. Example: the list of range of ten, zero and minus three. Ask each student to explain one answer in a single sentence to the neighbour, and then compare the two explanations.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python tutorial and the reference. The stories link to first-hand sources, and Python Tutor shows a loop step by step. Example: PEP 572 for the walrus. Ask the class to choose one link and read it before the next class.
